items.title: How to build a confident reader at home
items.author: Nusrat Jahan
items.alt: A parent and child reading together at home
items.excerpt: Small daily rituals can make reading feel like a natural part of childhood rather than another task.

body.text: Children who read confidently are rarely the ones who were pushed hardest. They are usually the ones for whom reading became a small, pleasant, repeating part of the day.

Parents often ask us what they can do at home to support the reading work happening in class. The honest answer is that the most powerful thing is not a programme or a workbook. It is ten unhurried minutes, most days, in the same comfortable place.
Make it a ritual, not a task

A ritual has a predictable shape. The same chair, the same time, the same opening line. When reading has a shape, children stop negotiating about whether it happens and start negotiating about what happens inside it: which books, which voices, which page they get to turn.

items: Pick a fixed moment: after dinner, before lights out, or straight after school.
Let your child choose the book, even if it is one you have read eleven times.
Read to them as often as they read to you. Listening is reading practice too.
Stop while it is still enjoyable. Ending on a good page is what makes tomorrow easy.

body.text: A child who associates reading with warmth will keep returning to it long after anyone is asking them to.
Let them see you do it

Children copy what they notice far more than what they are told. If reading is something the adults in the house visibly enjoy, it quietly becomes a normal, grown-up thing to do. A newspaper, a recipe, a message from a relative: anything with words in it counts.

body.title: Try this for one week
body.text: Put the phone in another room and keep a book on the table. You do not need to comment on it. Just let it be the thing that is there when everyone sits down.
What not to do

Avoid turning reading into an assessment. Asking a child to summarise every page, or correcting every mispronounced word immediately, turns a story into a test. Let small errors pass, finish the sentence, and come back to the sounds another day.

If a book is too hard, the pleasure disappears instantly. Reading something easier than their level is not a step backwards; it is how fluency gets built. In our classrooms we deliberately keep a range of levels within reach, so a child can choose a confident book on a tired day and a stretchy one on a bright one.
When to ask us for help

If your child is avoiding reading entirely, or if the same word is unrecognisable after many meetings, that is worth a conversation with their class teacher. We would much rather adjust early than let a small gap harden into a belief that reading is not for them.

items.title: Why digital literacy belongs in primary school
items.author: Md. Rafiq Hasan
items.alt: Children learning on computers in a classroom
items.excerpt: Children meet technology early either way. The question is whether they meet it with guidance.

body.text: Every child in our classrooms will grow up with technology woven through their work, their learning and their relationships. The only real choice is whether they meet it with guidance or on their own.

There is a common worry that bringing screens into a primary school means taking something away from childhood. We understand it. But the opposite has been our experience: when technology is taught deliberately, in short focused sessions with a clear purpose, children become far less fascinated by it and far more capable with it.
Digital literacy is not typing lessons

Digital literacy means knowing how to use a tool well, how to judge what it gives you, and how to behave towards people online. Those are thinking skills as much as technical ones. A child who can open a browser but cannot question what they find there has learned a small amount of software and no judgement at all.

items: Using a device purposefully, not just fluently.
Judging information: who made this, and why?
Creating something, not only consuming something.
Behaving safely and kindly with others online.

body.text: Coding as a way of thinking

Our coding sessions start long before formal syntax. Children sequence instructions, debug a set of steps, and break a big problem into small ones. When a child discovers that their robot turned left because they forgot a step, that is a genuine lesson in cause, effect and persistence.
By the time a child is old enough to write real code, the important thinking has already been practised.
body.cite: Md. Rafiq Hasan, Computer & IT Mentor

body.title: Age-appropriate by design
body.text: Session length, screen time and the activities themselves change with each class level. Younger children work in blocks, pictures and physical play; older children build, present and evaluate.
The question of screen time

We are not arguing for more screens. We are arguing for better ones. A twenty-minute session where a child builds something and explains it to a classmate is a very different act from an hour of passive scrolling, even though both involve a device.
What families can do

Ask to see what your child made, not just what they watched. Let them teach you something small. Keep devices in shared rooms at home. And when something strange or unkind appears online, treat it as a conversation rather than a crisis.
Guidance early is far easier than correction later. That is the whole argument for putting digital literacy in primary school, and it is why it sits alongside English and mathematics in ours.

items.title: A day inside the Edulife Innovation Lab
items.author: Md. Rafiq Hasan
items.alt: Students working in the Edulife Innovation Lab
items.excerpt: From first block-coding steps to a finished project — what a session in the lab really looks like.

body.text: The lab is rarely quiet. There is the click of laptops, a pair of children arguing politely about which block goes first, and someone at the back calling across the room because their sprite finally moved.
A session runs for a little under an hour and follows the same shape every time, so children always know what is coming.
The warm-up: eight minutes, no screens

We start with instructions told out loud. One child gives steps, another follows them literally. When the follower walks into a wall because nobody said turn, the room laughs and the lesson lands: computers do exactly what you say, not what you meant.
The build: thirty minutes, working in pairs

Today's class is making a simple quiz game. Pairs choose a subject, write three questions, and set up what happens when an answer is right or wrong. Nobody is given the finished code. They are given the pieces and a problem worth caring about.

items: Plan on paper first: what does the player see, and what happens next?
Build one piece at a time and test after every change.
When it breaks, read the steps back in order before changing anything.
Explain your working program to another pair at the end.

body.text: The moment a child says 'wait, it worked' is the moment they stop being a user and start being a maker.
body.cite: Md. Rafiq Hasan, Computer & IT Mentor

body.text: The share: fifteen minutes at the front

Every session ends with two or three pairs presenting. Presenting is not optional and it is not competitive. It is practice at explaining your own thinking, which is a skill children carry into every other subject.

body.title: What we look for
body.text: Not the most impressive project, but the most honest process. A child who can tell us what went wrong and how they fixed it has learned more than one who quietly copied the answer.
Why it matters beyond the lab

The habits that make a good lab session, planning before starting, testing, persisting through a bug, explaining your reasoning, are exactly the habits that make a good learner everywhere else. The lab is simply where they become visible.

items.title: Why questions are the beginning of learning
items.author: Topajjol Hossain Rasel
items.alt: A teacher answering a student's question in class
items.excerpt: A classroom where curiosity is welcomed produces learners who keep asking long after school.

body.text: A child asks roughly a hundred questions a day at four years old. Somewhere between then and secondary school, most of them stop. We think that is the single most avoidable loss in education.

Walk into one of our classrooms and you will hear questions from both directions. Children ask the teacher, and the teacher asks the class something they genuinely do not know the answer to. That second habit is the harder one to build, and it changes everything.
The fear of being wrong

By the time children reach Class 3, many have learned that a question is a risk. There is a right answer, the teacher has it, and guessing wrong has a cost. Once that belief sets in, hands go down and the classroom goes quiet in the worst possible way.

items: Praise the reasoning, even when the answer misses.
Ask 'how did you get there?' before 'is that right?'
Let a wrong answer sit and be examined instead of corrected instantly.
Answer honestly when you do not know, then find out together.

body.text: A child who has never been allowed to be wrong in front of others will never be brave enough to think out loud.
Questions as assessment

We learn more from a child's question than from their test score. 'Why does the moon follow the car?' tells you that a child is watching, wondering and willing to say so. That is the raw material every teacher wants.

body.title: A small habit worth copying
body.text: Keep a running 'question wall' in the classroom. Anything unanswered goes up there and gets visited on a Friday. It tells children that a good question outlives the lesson it was asked in.
What parents can do at home

When your child asks something you cannot answer, say so, plainly and comfortably. Then look it up together. The message is not that adults know everything. The message is that not knowing is a normal, ordinary, completely fine place to start.

items.title: Creating a calm homework routine
items.author: Razia Sultana Urmi
items.alt: A child working calmly at a desk at home
items.excerpt: When classwork is finished in class, home time can go back to being family time.

body.text: The evening hours are the most contested minutes in any family with a school-age child. We would like to give some of them back to you.

One of the pillars of Edulife is that classwork is completed in class. That is a deliberate design choice, not an accident of scheduling. It means that when your child comes home, the day's lesson has already been practised with a teacher nearby.
Why we timetable it this way

When work comes home unfinished, it lands on whoever happens to be available: usually tired, sometimes unsure of the method. Children quickly learn that they do not have to concentrate in class because someone will re-teach it later. Timetabling classwork into the school day removes both problems at once.

items: Focused practice happens while the lesson is still fresh.
Mistakes get corrected by the teacher who taught it.
Home time stays for rest, family and play.
Children build independence instead of dependence on an evening tutor.

body.text: Learning without dependence is not a slogan for us. It is a timetable decision.
What a useful home routine looks like
Even with classwork finished in class, most families still want some gentle structure at home. The aim is lightness.

items: A short reading slot: fifteen to twenty minutes, same time each day.
A quick look at the diary or notice board, together, once a day.
Some days, nothing at all. Rest is part of the routine, not a break from it.

body.title: If something takes too long
body.text: If an evening task is regularly stretching past twenty minutes, that is information, not a failure. Tell the class teacher. It usually means the level needs a small adjustment.
Household rhythm over perfect quiet

You do not need a silent study, a separate room or a special desk. A kitchen table while dinner cooks works perfectly well. What children remember is the feeling of the household settling around them, not the furniture.

items.title: Speaking up: phonetics in everyday practice
items.author: Nusrat Jahan
items.alt: A student speaking confidently in front of the class
items.excerpt: How short, frequent speaking moments build the confidence to address a room.

body.text: Confidence in front of a room is not a personality trait. It is a habit, and like any habit it is built in small, unremarkable repetitions.
We teach phonetics every day, in short bursts, from the earliest class. The aim is straightforward: clear sounds, a steady voice, and the willingness to speak even when the words are not perfect yet.
Why phonetics comes first

Pronunciation sits underneath every other English skill. A child who is unsure how a word sounds avoids using it, and a child who avoids words stops practising. Fix the sound and you unlock the vocabulary almost by accident.

items: Sound work happens in every class, not in a weekly special.
Children hear a model, copy it, then use it in a sentence.
Correction is quick, kind and specific: one thing at a time.
Every child speaks aloud every day, even for two sentences.

body.text: The goal is not a perfect accent. The goal is a child who is not afraid of their own voice.
From two sentences to a stage

The progression is gradual on purpose. A child might start by saying their news to the person sitting beside them. Later it is a sentence to the whole class, then a short prepared talk, then standing in front of families at our Young Speakers Showcase.

body.title: The 30-second rule
body.text: Every speaking task in the early years fits inside thirty seconds. Short tasks get finished and repeated often. Long tasks get dreaded.
At home: worth more than you think

Ask your child to tell you one thing that happened, out loud, without interruption. Then ask one follow-up question. That is it. Two minutes of undivided attention does more for spoken confidence than an hour of correction.
And when they mix languages, let it pass. Switching between Bangla and English is a sign of fluency in both, not confusion in either. The confidence comes first; the polish comes with time.

items.title: What we learned from our first coding showcase
items.author: Tanvir Chowdhury
items.excerpt: Twelve projects, one afternoon, and a much clearer picture of what children can build.

body.text: Twelve projects, one afternoon, and about sixty children explaining their own work to anyone who stopped long enough to listen. We learned more in three hours than in a term of assessment sheets.

The showcase was not a competition. There were no rankings and no first prize. Every child stood beside their own project and answered questions about it, which turned out to be the most revealing part of the whole afternoon.
What surprised us
The most impressive projects were not the most technically complex. They were the ones where a child could explain every decision, including the decisions that went wrong.

items: Children who struggled most in lessons often explained their work best.
The simplest projects held visitors' attention the longest.
Almost every child could describe one bug they had fixed and how.
Working in pairs produced noticeably more confident explanations.

body.text: We stopped asking 'what did you make?' and started asking 'tell me about this part here'. The answers changed completely.
What we will change next time

We are extending the explanation time and shortening the display time. We are also adding a simple written reflection beside each project: three sentences on what was hard and what they would do differently, so the thinking is captured alongside the artefact.

body.title: A useful principle
body.text: If a child can only show you their finished project but not describe the process, they have learned a result. If they can describe the process, they have learned a method they can reuse.
Why we will keep doing it

Public explanation changes what children believe about themselves. Standing next to something you built, answering a stranger's question, discovering that you actually do know why it works: that is where confidence comes from. We will be running a showcase every term.

items.title: Building a school community that lasts
items.author: Amir Hossain Rozel
items.alt: Families and students at a school community event
items.excerpt: Community is not an event on the calendar — it is what happens between them.

body.text: When we opened the first Edulife campus, we thought a community was something you built with events. A decade later we know it is the opposite. Events are where a community becomes visible. It is built in the ordinary days in between.

What makes a school feel like somewhere a family belongs? It is rarely the size of the campus or the number of activities on the notice board. It is whether people recognise each other, and whether they feel expected.
The small things that carry the most weight

items: A teacher who greets a child by name at the gate, every morning.
A parent who is told, specifically, about something their child did that week.
A visitor who is met, not just processed.
A problem that is raised and then actually resolved, visibly.

body.text: Trust is built in small moments of ordinary reliability, long before anyone needs to rely on it in a difficult one.
Two campuses, one culture

Running Khagrachari and Luxmichari as one school rather than two has been deliberate from the start. Teachers meet across campuses, our curriculum and standards are shared, and children from both sites meet at showcases, fairs and the annual carnival.

body.title: Our commitment to families
body.text: If something is not working, we want to hear it while it is still small. Every message to the school office gets a reply within one working day. That promise is the beginning of every other one.
What we are building toward

We want children to leave Edulife with strong foundations, a confident voice, and a clear sense that learning belongs to them. We want families to feel that they were part of the building. And we want the school to still be standing on the same principles in another decade.
